items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on d4 can move to.

claims.statement: The white knight on d4 can legally go to exactly these seven squares.

hints: Stuck? That is fine: read on, because the next card and board work through this very position. First picture the eight squares an L away from d4.
A square holding a white piece is crossed out. A square holding a black piece stays in, because the knight can capture there.
Seven squares are right. The one eight-candidate square missing is c2, where a white pawn stands.
items.explain: The knight on d4 has eight candidate squares: b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, e6, f3 and f5. Only c2 is crossed out, because a white pawn stands there. The black pawn on b5, the rook on c6, the bishop on e6 and the pawn on f5 can all be captured, so those squares stay in. The white pawns on c2 and e3 block nothing, because a knight jumps.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on f3 can jump to.

claims.statement: The white knight on f3 can legally go to exactly these five squares.

hints: Write down the eight squares an L away from f3, then check each one.
d2, g1 and h2 hold white pieces, so they are crossed out. The pawn on e5 is a black piece.
Five squares are right: the ones on the d-file, e-file, g-file and h-file that are free or hold an enemy piece.
items.explain: From f3 the eight candidates are d2, d4, e1, e5, g1, g5, h2 and h4. White pieces stand on d2 (pawn), g1 (king) and h2 (pawn), so those three are crossed out. The other five stay in, and e5 is a capture of a black pawn. Pieces next to the knight, such as the pawn on e4, do not matter.

items.prompt: How many squares can the white knight on a1 jump to? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The knight on a1 can go to exactly c2.

hints: A knight in the corner has two candidate squares. Name them.
One of the two candidate squares holds a white pawn.
b3 is taken by the pawn, so only one jump is left.
items.explain: In the corner the knight on a1 has two candidates, b3 and c2. The white pawn stands on b3, so that jump is crossed out. Only c2 is left. A corner knight with one friendly piece next to it can be down to one jump.

items.prompt: Black to move. The white queen attacks the piece on h5. Can it jump to a square that no white piece attacks? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The queen attacks the knight on h5.
The knight on h5 can go to exactly f4, f6 and g3.
A white pawn attacks f4.
A white pawn attacks f6.
A white pawn attacks g3.

hints: The knight is on the edge. Count its jumps first, then ask what attacks each landing square.
g7 holds a black pawn, so that jump is crossed out. Look at the white pawns on e3, e5 and h2.
Each of the three remaining landing squares is attacked by a white pawn.
items.explain: The knight on h5 can reach f4, f6 and g3; g7 holds its own pawn. The pawn on e3 attacks f4, the pawn on e5 attacks f6, and the pawn on h2 attacks g3. Every jump lands next to a pawn that can take it, while the queen already attacks the knight where it stands. The knight cannot escape: every jump lands where a pawn takes it, and the queen already attacks it where it stands.

items.prompt: Black to move, in check. Can Black escape by moving a piece other than the king? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
No black piece attacks the knight on e7.
Black has exactly three legal moves, all with the king.

hints: A knight check cannot be blocked, because the jump has nothing in between.
The other way out of a check is to take the checking piece. Does any black piece attack e7?
No black piece attacks e7, so only the king can move.
items.explain: The knight on e7 attacks the king on g8. A knight check has no squares in between, so a piece cannot step into the way. The only other answer is to capture the knight, and neither the rook on d8 nor the bishop on d7 attacks e7. So Black must move the king, to f7, f8 or h8.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the knight jump that gives check and attacks the rook at the same time.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to c7.
After the jump the knight attacks the king.
After the jump the knight attacks the rook.
The jump wins the rook.
After b5d6 the knight does not attack the rook.

hints: A double attack needs two targets in the knight's eight jumps. Look at the black king and the black rook on a6.
Find a landing square that is an L away from both e8 and a6.
The square is c7: it is an L from a6 and also an L from e8.
items.explain: From c7 the knight attacks the king on e8 and the rook on a6 at once. Black must answer the check, and then the knight takes the rook. The jump to d6 also gives check, but from d6 the knight attacks only the pawn on f7 and the king, so the rook on a6 is safe.

feedback_by_move.b5d6: This also gives check, but from d6 the knight does not attack the rook on a6.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap the landing squares for the knight on c3 where it cannot be captured.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has exactly six legal jumps.
A black pawn attacks a4.
A black pawn attacks b5.
A black pawn attacks d5.
No black pawn attacks b1.
No black pawn attacks d1.
No black pawn attacks e2.

hints: First find the six legal landing squares; e4 is crossed out because a white pawn stands there.
A black pawn attacks the squares diagonally in front of it, toward the white side. Which landing squares are those?
The pawn on b5 attacks a4, and the pawn on c6 attacks b5 and d5. The other three squares are free of pawn attacks.
items.explain: The knight on c3 can jump to a4, b1, b5, d1, d5 and e2. The black pawn on b5 attacks a4, and the pawn on c6 attacks b5 and d5. So those three landing squares are attacked by a pawn. Only b1, d1 and e2 are free of pawn attacks, and all three are steps backward.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on e5 can move to.

claims.statement: The white knight on e5 can legally go to exactly these six squares.

hints: First decide what kind of piece stands on e5, then recall how it moves.
It jumps. White pieces on c4 and g4 are on two of its landing squares; black pieces can be captured.
Six squares are right. The rook on d7 and the pawn on f7 are both on landing squares.
items.explain: The piece on e5 is a knight. Its eight candidates are c4, c6, d3, d7, f3, f7, g4 and g6. White pawns stand on c4 and g4, so those two are crossed out. The black rook on d7 and the black pawn on f7 can be captured, so they stay in. Six jumps remain.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on c4 can move to.

claims.statement: The white bishop on c4 can legally go to exactly these seven squares.

hints: First decide what kind of piece stands on c4. It does not jump this time.
A bishop slides along diagonals and stops before its own pieces. Where does the white pawn on d3 block it?
Seven squares: a2 and b3 on one diagonal, b5 and a6 on another (a6 is a capture), d5, e6 and f7 on a third (f7 is a capture).
items.explain: The piece on c4 is a bishop, so it slides along diagonals. The white pawn on d3 blocks the way down to the right, but the other three directions are open. It can go to b3 and a2, to b5 and a6 (a capture), and to d5, e6 and f7 (a capture). A bishop is stopped by what is in between; a knight is not.

items.prompt: Black to move. How many squares can the piece on g8 move to? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The black knight on g8 can go to exactly f6 and h6.

hints: Name the piece on g8 first. Then list its candidate squares and cross out the ones off the board.
From g8 the three jumps that stay on the board are e7, f6 and h6. One of them holds a black pawn.
The pawn on e7 is its own, so f6 and h6 remain.
items.explain: The piece on g8 is a knight on the edge. Of its eight jumps only e7, f6 and h6 stay on the board. The black pawn on e7 takes e7 away, so two jumps remain: f6 and h6.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the jump to a central square where no black pawn can take the knight.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to e4.
No black pawn attacks e4.
Two black pawns attack d5.

hints: Two central squares are open to the knight. Check what attacks each before you choose.
One of them is attacked by two black pawns.
The other one is free of pawn attacks.
items.explain: The knight can reach d5 and e4, both in the centre. The pawns on c6 and e6 both attack d5, so a pawn takes the knight there. Nothing attacks e4, so the knight lands safely. A legal jump is not always a safe one.

feedback_by_move.c3d5: d5 is attacked by two black pawns, so a pawn takes the knight.
feedback_by_move.c3b5: The pawn on c6 takes the knight on b5.
